How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, (the "appellant") appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) issued on June 24, 2015 with the written Notice of Decision being issued on June 25, 2015, accepting the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "respondent"), a citizen of Libya , for refugee protection.

New evidence has been submitted by the appellant and pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act"),1 the appellant seeks to have the new evidence entered in this appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (the "RAD").
The respondent has also submitted new evidence pursuant to sections 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act.
Neither the appellant2 nor the respondent3 seeks a hearing pursuant to section 110(6) of the Act.
The appellant asks the RAD to set aside the determination of the RPD and order the matter be returned to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted Panel.4
The respondent asks the RAD to confirm the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention refugee.
Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention refugee. This appeal is dismissed.
The respondent is a citizen of Libya. While living in Libya he was a small XXXX XXXX business owner in the city of XXXX.

In XXXX 2013 he was interviewed by a XXXX XXXX from the XXXX XXXX "XXXX XXXX" (or XXXX XXXX). During this interview he expressed negative opinions about the state of affairs in Libya focusing specifically on the negative influence of religious extremists groups and singling out the militia group known as Ansar al-Sharia for criticism. The respondent was excited about finally being able to express his opinions in a public forum.

The respondent was interviewed in his store. By coincidence the director of this XXXX project was a friend of the respondent, named XXXX XXXX XXXX. The interview had not been pre-arranged and it was only by chance that the respondent was approached to be interviewed for the "man on the street" style interview by Mr. XXXX.

A fellow merchant named XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was also interviewed and he too expressed the same type of negative opinions about religious extremist groups in general and Ansar al-Sharia in particular. The XXXX XXXX in Libya several days after the interviews.

Not long after the interview the respondent received a visitor's visa for Canada enabling him to travel to Canada to attend his brother's wedding. The issue date for the visa was XXXX XXXX, 2013 and the expiry date was XXXX XXXX, 2014.5 The respondent travelled to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013.

In XXXX 2014, while still in Canada he received word that XXXX XXXX XXXX had been murdered in XXXX 2014 by members of Ansar al-Sharia. He also learned that one of his employees had been kidnapped and beaten by members of Ansar al-Sharia who had come to his store looking for the respondent. His brother informed him that members of Ansar al-Sharia had come to their house looking for him as well. They apparently threatened to kill him.
As a result of the threats to his life the respondent sought refugee protection in Canada on or about March 3, 2015.

The appellant has not specifically identified the issues for this appeal under its own heading. The RAD has reviewed the appellant's memo and has identified the following issues in support of his application to have the RAD set aside the RPD decision. 1) Is the RPD decision unreasonable by virtue of not making clear findings on determinative issues in particular the threat to the respondent by Ansar-al-Sharia in XXXX?6 2) Did the RPD conduct a faulty analysis when assessing the suitability of XXXX as an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA).7 3) Did the RPD err in law by shifting the burden of proof from the respondent to the appellant?8 NEW EVIDENCE Appellant

The appellant has submitted the following new evidence and seeks to have it entered as evidence in this RAD appeal pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Act. 1) A Declaration dated August 18, 2015 from CBSA Officer Diana Gunadi;9 2) A copy of a death certificate with the name and pertinent details of the deceased redacted;10 3) A new interpretation of a medical report allegedly issued by the XXXX Hospital in XXXX, Libya and signed by Dr. XXXX XXXX XXXX11 that was entered in evidence at the RPD hearing.12 The new interpretation was completed by Hossein Talebian an accredited translator. Respondent

The respondent has submitted the following new evidence and seeks to have it entered as evidence in this RAD appeal pursuant to section 110(3) and 110(5) of the Act:13 4) An article published by The Long War Journal - A Project of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies entitled "Ansar al Sharia Libya fights on under new leader". Published June 30, 2015. 5) Security statement from Government of Canada, "Embassy of Canada to Libya." Last modified June 12, 2015.
Neither the appellant nor the respondent made submissions with respect to the standard of review the RAD should apply to the assessment of the RPD decision.

While the Act sets out grounds for appeal, as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the RPD. The first Federal Court (the "Court") review of a RAD decision was in May 2014 (Iyamuremye).14 Since that time there has been a number of Court decisions rendered. It is fair to say that, to a large extent, the Court is not of one mind as to the standard of review that the RAD should apply. The majority of decisions have made one thing clear, however, and that is, the RAD should not apply "reasonableness" as its standard of review. Until such time as the Federal Court of Appeal (the "FCA") brings more clarity to the standard of review I take the Court's direction on this issue and do not apply the standard of reasonableness to this appeal.

I have examined the various Court decisions regarding the role of the RAD and find that the process of a hybrid appeal proposed by Mr. Justice Phelan in Huruglica15 is consistent with the common thread found in the majority of the Court decisions that state the RAD must comprehensively review the available relevant evidence when assessing the RPD's findings and come to an assessment of the appellant's refugee claim. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

Mr. Justice Phelan determined that, in conducting its assessment, the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. The RAD is, however, not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on the facts only where there is "palpable and overriding error".

In keeping with the majority of the Court's findings, I undertook to examine and review all the evidence in the RPD Record (RPDR) and, unless otherwise stated, conducted my own independent assessment of the evidence and came to my own conclusion based on that evidence. ANALYSIS Admissibility of New Evidence Presented on Appeal

Section 110(3) of the Act, states the RAD may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and the person who is subject of the appeal. Section 110(4) of the Act directs that the person subject of the appeal may only present evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or evidence that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of rejection. Section 110(5) states that this section does not apply in respect of evidence that is presented in response to evidence presented by the Minister.
Section 171(a.5) states that the Minister may submit documentary evidence and make written submissions in support of the Minister's appeal at any time before the RAD makes a decision.

Madam Justice Gagné found in the matter of Singh16 that section 110(4) of the Act must be applied by the RAD with sufficient flexibility so as not to hinder the full fact-based appeal the RAD is mandated to conduct. Mr. Justice Barnes strongly endorsed this finding in Sow.17

The law is unsettled on this issue as well. Madam Justice Strickland recently found in the matter of Deri:18 [60] By contrast, s. 110(4) offers the RAD no discretion to refuse to apply its explicit admissibility requirements for new evidence. The provision enumerates the factors that the RAD must apply, thereby determining the result based on the facts of the case. If the new evidence meets the requirements of s. 110(4) then the RAD must accept it. Conversely, if it does not, then the RAD must reject it. While there is an element of subjectivity in assessing whether the evidence was reasonably available or if an applicant could not reasonably been expected to have previously presented it, this is a factual assessment, it does not alter the character of the ultimate decision as to admissibility. Accordingly, in my view, the RAD's interpretation of s. 110(4) was reasonable.

Many RAD Members have applied the criteria as set out in Raza19 as the standard for the acceptance of new evidence. The Court has, in some of their reviews of the RAD decisions, determined that the factors set out in the Raza decision do not apply to the RAD in its capacity of an appeal division.

Raza dealt with a pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) but the wording in the legislation enshrines the same legal test as set out in section 110(4). In Raza the FCA identified credibility, newness, relevance, and materiality as issues to be considered. As with the RAD standard of review issue, there is no comity within the Court regarding following the jurisprudence as set out in Raza. Mr. Justice Mosley stated in Denbel:20 [42] In Khachatourian above21 at para 37, Justice Simon Noël expressed reservations about the propriety of transposing Raza to the RAD context, referring to the analysis of Justice Gagné in Singh v. Canada. . . . Once again I respectfully disagree. . . . [43] When interpreting legislative intent, the Court must give priority to the written text in the absence of any lexical ambiguity. The Court's opinions on best policy cannot supplant the text of the law; nor can select passages from the Hansard. In my view, Parliament intended these two provisions to enshrine the same legal test. If Parliament had intended to establish more flexible admissibility rules in RAD appeals, it would not have replicated the restrictive language which governs PRRAs.
Competing findings such as those identified above, all binding on the RAD, place RAD Members on the "horns of a dilemma."

Until such time as the FCA brings clarity to this issue, when applying the conditions for new evidence as set out in section 110(4) of the Act and section 29(4) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (the "RAD Rules"),22 I will consider whether exclusion of the proposed evidence would hinder a full fact based review of the appeal and at the same time will respect and apply the legislation that governs the acceptance of new evidence. The factors as identified in Raza will be used as a guide and will be applied with flexibility. If applied properly I do not find these guiding principles to be mutually exclusive. Appellant's New Evidence

Under normal circumstances there would be no analysis required for documents entered by the Minister as section 171(a.5) gives the Minister statutory authority to enter documentary evidence at any time before the RAD renders its decision. This matter, however, is unique and an analysis of the declaration of Officer Gunadi, which is put forward by the Minister as new evidence, is required.

In her declaration Officer Gunadi does not specifically state that Mr. Talebian was the interpreter for the respondent's RPD hearing but does make reference to him reviewing the medical report at the hearing. The RPDR clearly establishes that Mr. Talebian was the interpreter at the respondent's RPD hearing.

Officer Gunadi states in her declaration that Mr. Talebain advised her that the medical report was poorly written and not consistent with medical documents he had interpreted in the past. He stated that the document does not appear to be written by an educated individual. He also offered his opinion that it is odd that a doctor would include information pertaining to Ansar al-Sharia as normally medical reports only includes medical information.

The RAD reviewed the audio recording of the RPD hearing and noted that the RPD adjourned for what the Member described as a five minute break23 but did not turn off the recording. The conversation in the room thus became part of the RPDR. Mr. Talebain can be heard telling the Minister's representative that the medical document is poorly written and not the writing of an educated person.24 Officer Gunadi also makes reference to this conversation in her declaration.

The Minister is given statutory authority by virtue of section 171(a.5) to submit documentary evidence or make written submissions at any time before the RAD has rendered it's decision, this authorization, however, is not absolute. The circumstances surrounding the proposed submission of the declaration of Officer Gunadi (Minister's new evidence No. 1) is troubling to this RAD. The content of this document leads the RAD to conclude that the interpreter abandoned his duty to be impartial. The interpreter's role in the hearing is to interpret accurately, to the best of his ability. He is not to give evidence or offer his conclusions of the evidence either before the RPD or in private to counsel.

The actions of the interpreter may have violated Immigration and Refugee Board (the "IRB") Code of Conduct for interpreters when he offered his unsolicited opinion regarding the authenticity of the medical report, to Minister's counsel.25 The Code of Conduct states in part: . . . Interpreter Service Contractors shall be, and shall appear to be, objective and impartial at all times, inside or outside the conference or hearing room, in relation to any matter for which they provide services to the Board. . . ."

It is this RAD's opinion that it was also not appropriate for Minister's counsel, firstly, to have listened to the interpreter give his opinion and once having heard him not to have revealed the conversation to the Presiding Member and Counsel for the respondent. Secondly, as an officer of the Court, the RAD expects Minister's counsel to be aware of, and follow, proper procedure. It is not appropriate to use the individual who interpreted in the respondent's hearing to give evidence in an adversarial process in support of the Minister's appeal which argues against the positive determination of the RPD. In doing so the Minister's representative was placing the interpreter in a position where, if he co-operates with the Minister, he could be violating the IRB Code of Conduct.

The interpreter's role in the RPD hearing is a vital one. The respondent has the right to expect that the interpreter will be impartial26 and not act as an agent for the Minister. The respondent further has the right to expect that the interpreter will adhere to the Code of Conduct of the IRB. Although it will be up to the administrative process of the IRB to determine if the interpreter violated the IRB Code of Conduct it is the responsibility of this RAD to determine if the proposed evidence is so tainted by the circumstances leading up to the appellant obtaining it, that the respondent's right to fundamental justice and procedural fairness would be violated if the appellant's exhibit No. 1 is accepted as evidence in this appeal.

Having carefully considered the facts surrounding the appellant obtaining the evidence contained in Officer Gunadi's declaration I find that there was a breach in procedural fairness and/or natural justice in the manner the evidence was obtained and the fact that the interrupter at the RPD hearing was the same person giving the evidence which is meant to discredit the respondent.

The Court recently dealt with a similar issue in the matter of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v. Paramo de Gutierrez.27 In Gutierrez the Court upheld a RAD decision that CBSA breached procedural fairness by not respecting Mr. Gutierrez's right to counsel. The Court also upheld the RAD finding that the RPD breached procedural fairness when it did not exclude evidence obtained by CBSA after the breach.

In this case, this RAD has determined that the Minister breached procedural fairness by using the interpreter who was utilized during the RPD hearing, to obtain evidence that is intended to be used to discredit the respondent. The jurisprudence and natural justice dictate that the RAD would err if it did not exclude the evidence obtained as a result of that breach.

I find that should the appellant's new evidence no.1 be accepted in this appeal it would amount to a breach of fundamental justice and/or procedural fairness. For the foregoing reasons and notwithstanding section 171(a.5) of the Act, the RAD rejects the new evidence No. 1 in this appeal.
New evidence No. 2 and No. 3 are accepted pursuant to section 171(a.5) of the Act. Respondent's New Evidence

The proposed new evidence for the respondent is in response to the new evidence submitted by the appellant therefore pursuant to section 110(5) of the Act the respondent's new evidence No. 4 and No. 5 are accepted for this appeal.

Section 110(3) of the Act directs the RAD, with certain exceptions, to proceed without a hearing on the basis of the record of proceedings from the RPD. Section 110(6) states the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, the documentary evidence referred to in section (3): a. raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is subject of the appeal; b. is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim and, c. if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

Neither party has requested a hearing in this matter. The new evidence accepted in this appeal does deal with credibility but forms only part of the evidence that would be considered in an overall credibility assessment and therefore, in and by itself, would not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.
No hearing will be ordered in this matter. THE RPD'S FINDING REGARDING THE THREAT OF ANSAR al-SHARIA IN TRIPOLI

The appellant states that the RPD decision is unreasonable as it does not make clear findings on issues or provide sufficient analysis when assessing the threat of Ansar al-Sharia to the respondent in XXXX.

In particular the appellant states the RPD erred in fact when it relied on the information contained in the United Kingdom Home Office Operational Guidance note published in May 2013.28 The appellant submits that the information contained in this document was "dated" and more accurate information was contained in the document it submitted as evidence by the appellant. This document is entitled "The Rise and Decline of Ansar al-Sharia in Libya" and is dated April 6, 2015 and authored by Aaron Y. Zelin (Zelin article).29

The information the appellant submits that is contained in the newer document and not in the Home Office report, is that the power and influence of Ansar al-Sharia was fading and in order to survive have joined other Islamic groups, and that the RPD erred when it concluded that the group was expanding by virtue of mergers with these other fundamental Islamic factions.

I disagree with the appellant that the RPD erred in its assessment of the evidence. The RPD dealt with its analysis of this evidence in its Reasons under the heading "Well-Founded Fear of Persecution and the Lack of State Protection." I note that it used information from the Zelin article to conclude that Ansar al-Sharia had joined forces with other Islamic factions under the banner of Majlis Shura Thuwar Benghazi (MSTB, the Benghazi Revolutionaries Consultative Council). The alliance was announced on June 20, 2014.30 The evidence does not establish that MSTB and/or Ansar al-Sharia is restricted to certain areas of Libya, nor does it establish that areas of operation such as Tripoli are out of reach for them.

I have reviewed the evidence in this matter including the Zelin article. I cannot agree with the appellant that the Zelin article establishes on the balance of probabilities that Ansar al-Sharia is no longer a threat to the respondent in Tripoli. The article states that MSTB (of which Ansar al-Sharia is part of) remains a potent force to this day.31 The article also states there are a number of outstanding issues regarding Ansar al-Sharia that only the future will reveal. One of those issues is whether or not Ansar al-Sharia will maintain its independence or slowly merge with the other military outfits.32 This certainly does not establish that Ansar al-Sharia does not currently control its own military objectives. The article also states it remains to be seen if Ansar al-Sharia can sustain operations in cities beyond its Benghazi base.33 This does not establish that Ansar al-Sharia is not capable of operating in other cities including Tripoli. According to the article, these and other issues it identified, remain to be determined.

This is the appellant's own evidence and to suggest that it establishes that Ansar al Sharia is no longer a serious threat to the respondent in Tripoli, or any other part of Libya for that matter, is not supported by this evidence or other evidence entered at the RPD hearing or this RAD appeal.

There is insufficient credible evidence before me to find that Ansar al-Sharia has lost its influence by virtue of the merger. The evidence is that a merger has occurred and rather than the groups influence deteriorating it is equally as possible that the merger has strengthened the group, as it is now part of a larger organization that is the sum of several like-minded parts. This is the conclusion that the RPD came to after it assessed the evidence, a conclusion the appellant obviously disagrees with but that does make it an error in fact.

The RPD finding is strengthened by the respondent's new evidence No. 4, the article published by The Long War Journal - A Project of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies entitled: "Ansar al- Sharia Libya fights on under new leader". The inescapable conclusion after reviewing this evidence is that Ansar al-Sharia is still very active in Libya and is not restricted from operating in any particular area of Libya.

Having conducted its own independent analysis, this RAD concurs with the RPD finding regarding the threat that Answar al-Sharia poses to the respondent in every part of Libya and finds that there is more than a reasonable chance that the respondent would face persecution in all parts of Libya. IS THE RPD DECISION UNREASONABLE BY VIRTUE OF NOT MAKING CLEAR FINDINGS DETERMINATIVE ISSUES? - CREDIBILITY

The appellant identifies two areas of concern regarding the evidence. The appellant states the RPD erred in fact by ignoring the viva voce evidence of the respondent and the evidence contained in the National Documentation Package regarding the issuance of a death certificate and a burial permit. The documentary evidence states that a death must be registered within twenty-four hours and that there is a specific form that must be drawn up.34 The appellant quotes the RPD Reasons that state, the RPD did not have any evidence that indicates the family of the deceased had a need for the medical report before being asked by the claimant to provide him with evidence to support his claim for refugee protection.35 The appellant does not identify the significance of this in his memorandum, but the RPD dealt with this issue under "Credibility Concerns" and so I conclude that the appellant is identifying this to the RAD in an effort to establish the respondent was not credible regarding his claim.

The appellant also submits that the witness, Mr. Sanussi, and the respondent were not consistent regarding their evidence as to how they first met. The RPD acknowledged this inconsistency but concluded that it was not unusual for two men who frequented the same social circle to forget where and how they first met.

In keeping with the Court's finding I take notice that the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion.36 I afford the RPD such recognition and respect regarding its finding regarding the credibility of the respondent in the matter before me.

It is the RPD that is in the best position to make a finding on credibility as it was the RPD who had the appellant before it and was able to observe the appellant and question him on credibility related issues37. This is the only deference I afford the RPD regarding this appeal.
The Court has stated that analyzing findings of fact and determinations of credibility fall within the heartland of the RPD expertise.38

Although it would have been preferable if the RPD dealt specifically with the documentary evidence in the NDP regarding the issuing of death and burial certificates as it related to the matter before it, I find that the RPD did not ignore the evidence. The respondent was questioned on it and stated that he simply did not know why the issuance date on the evidence was not the same as the date of death. He also testified that he had no knowledge as to why there would be two different issuing authorities on the document, one from the Ministry of Defense and one from the Ministry of Health.

The RPD dealt with the weight it placed on these discrepancies in its Reasons. It is not necessary for me to restate in different words what the RPD adequately explained in its decision.39 The RPD clearly set out what inconsistencies it was concerned with and why it did not find them to be persuasive in challenging the respondent's credibility.

I have reviewed the entire record and find the RPD decision to be logical, solidly based on the evidence before it and in keeping with existing jurisprudence. I defer to the RPD regarding its finding regarding the credibility of the respondent. SHIFTING OF BURDEN OF PROOF TO THE MINISTER

It is trite law that states the burden of proof in a refugee protection matter is on the respondent. The appellant argues that the RPD shifted this burden onto the Minister and identifies language used by the RPD in its Reasons in support of this argument.

It is unfortunate that the words "the Minister has not established" are used in the RPD Reasons as these words are open to misinterpretation. I do not agree, however, that the use of these words establishes that the RPD shifted the burden of proof to the Minister.

The RAD recognizes the level of expertise that the RPD has. It is incomprehensible to this RAD that the RPD would not know and apply such a basic principle as the burden of proof to its decision making.

The appellant has misinterpreted the meaning of these words in the context of the RPD decision. This RAD concludes that the RPD is stating that the appellant made no submissions regarding state protection or internal flight alternative (IFA) inferring that if there was a viable IFA and/or adequate state protection available the appellant would have made submissions in this regard. This is a legitimate consideration when addressing these two issues.

This RAD notes that the Minister's representative advised the RPD that in his opinion state protection was not an issue at the refugee protection hearing.40 It is difficult for the appellant to now argue that he has somehow been prejudiced by the RPD applying the wrong standard of review on an issue that he determined was not relevant in the refugee claim.

The appellant further submits that the RPD stated that the Minister has not established a lack of subjective fear. Once again, I find the wording to be unfortunate but do not agree with the appellant that it indicates that the RPD was shifting the burden of proof to the Minister. Examining this statement in the context of the entire set of Reasons, this RAD concludes that the RPD was analyzing the issue of subjective fear in light of the Minister's submission. What the RPD is saying is that the Minister's arguments were not persuasive enough to move the RPD from its determination that the respondent did establish a subjective fear at his RPD hearing. This is within the mandate of the RPD and totally proper in the decision making process.
For the above reasons the RAD confirms the RPD decision.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the respondent is a Convention Refugee. This appeal is dismissed. (signed) "Gordon C. McRae" Gordon C.
